method: Each S1 claim checked against the retrieved text of the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis)' (last updated September 2024, PIC endorsed) and machine-checked verbatim with scripts/verify.py. S2 claims were read from the croup management diagram image, carry verdict pass_image_transcription and cannot be machine re-checked. TWO clinically material items exist only in the diagram and nowhere in the guideline text: nebulised budesonide 2 mg where oral corticosteroids are not tolerated, and a repeat steroid dose the following evening in mild and moderate croup. The diagram also specifies the adrenaline as UNDILUTED, which the text does not. Nebulised adrenaline volume is stated in the text only for life-threatening croup. Source URLs were recorded at retrieval.

claims.claim: Clinicians should minimise distress to the child as this can worsen upper airway obstruction
claims.source_text: 1. Minimise distress to the child, as this can worsen upper airway obstruction

claims.claim: Senior staff should be involved early and transfer considered if there are concerns regarding worsening upper airway obstruction
claims.source_text: 2. Involve senior staff early and consider transfer if concerns regarding worsening upper airway obstruction

claims.claim: For severe and life-threatening croup, nebulised adrenaline should be used and a skilled senior clinician sought for airway support, while less severe cases can be managed with corticosteroids alone
claims.source_text: 3. For severe and life-threatening croup, use nebulised adrenaline and seek a skilled senior clinician for airway support … 4. Less severe cases can be managed with corticosteroids alone

claims.claim: Croup is inflammation of the upper airway, larynx and trachea usually triggered by a virus, most commonly parainfluenza as well as other respiratory viruses including COVID-19, occurs generally between the ages of 6 months and 6 years, and is often worse at night
claims.source_text: Croup is inflammation of the upper airway, larynx and trachea, usually triggered by a virus, most commonly parainfluenza as well as other respiratory viruses including COVID-19 (apply appropriate infection control) … Occurs generally between the ages of 6 months and 6 years … Often worse at night

claims.claim: Children with croup should have a focused examination so as not to upset them further
claims.source_text: Children with croup should have focused examination so as not to upset them further:

claims.claim: Observations such as oximetry and blood pressure are not necessary for managing croup and can be omitted if expected to cause distress, throat examination is rarely required, and the child should be kept with the carer with the carer involved in assisting with examination
claims.source_text: Observations such as oximetry and blood pressure are not necessary for managing croup, and can be omitted if expected to cause distress … Throat examination is rarely required … Keep child with carer and involve the carer in assisting with examination

claims.claim: Risk factors for severe croup include history of previous severe croup, pre-existing narrowing of upper airways, reduced airway tone due to pre-existing conditions such as trisomy 21 or neuromuscular conditions, and young age noting croup is uncommon under 6 months and rare under 3 months in which case an alternative diagnosis should be considered
claims.source_text: Risk factors for severe croup include: … History of previous severe croup … Pre-existing narrowing of upper airways … Reduced airway tone due to pre-existing conditions eg trisomy 21, neuromuscular conditions … Young age: uncommon in under 6 months old, rare in under 3 months old. Consider alternative diagnosis

claims.claim: Examination findings include barking cough, stridor, hoarse voice or cry, possible associated widespread wheeze, increased work of breathing, and possible fever but no signs of toxicity
claims.source_text: Barking cough … Stridor … Hoarse voice or cry … May have associated widespread wheeze … Increased work of breathing … May have fever, but no signs of toxicity

claims.claim: Loudness of stridor is not a good indicator of severity of obstruction, and soft stridor in the presence of a worsening clinical picture may be a sign of imminent airway obstruction
claims.source_text: Loudness of stridor is not a good indicator of severity of obstruction. Soft stridor in the presence of worsening clinical picture may be a sign of imminent airway obstruction

claims.claim: In the severity table appearance and colour runs from normal and well-perfused in mild and moderate, to pale in severe, to pale, mottled or cyanosed in life-threatening
claims.source_text: | **Appearance/colour** | Normal, well-perfused | Normal, well-perfused | Pale | Pale, mottled or cyanosed |

claims.claim: Behaviour runs from alert and active in mild, to alert and active with intermittent mild agitation in moderate, to increasing agitation and drowsiness in severe, to confused, drowsy, agitated and possibly not moving or drooling in life-threatening
claims.source_text:
| **Behaviour** | Alert and active | Alert and active, intermittent mild agitation | Increasing agitation, drowsiness | Confused, drowsy, agitated
May be not moving, drooling |

claims.claim: Stridor runs from none or only when active or upset in mild, to intermittent at rest in moderate, to persistent at rest or biphasic in severe, to biphasic or may be soft in life-threatening
claims.source_text:
| **Stridor** | None, or only when active or upset | Intermittent at rest | Persistent at rest,
or biphasic\* | Biphasic or may be soft |

claims.claim: Respiratory rate runs from normal in mild, to increased in moderate, to marked increase or decrease in severe, to abnormal with signs of impending respiratory exhaustion in life-threatening
claims.source_text: | **Respiratory rate** | Normal | Increased | Marked increase or decrease | Abnormal, signs of impending respiratory exhaustion |

claims.claim: Accessory muscle use runs from none or minimal in mild, to intercostal and subcostal recession with tracheal tug in moderate, to abdominal breathing with marked recession and tracheal tug in severe, to severe sternal recession with exhaustion and poor respiratory effort in life-threatening
claims.source_text: | **Accessory muscle use** | None or minimal | Intercostal and subcostal recession, tracheal tug | Abdominal breathing, marked intercostal and subcostal recession, tracheal tug | Severe sternal recession, exhausted, poor respiratory effort |

claims.claim: Oxygen saturation is normal in mild and moderate croup, and hypoxia is a late sign which may indicate imminent complete upper airway obstruction
claims.source_text: | **Oxygen saturation** | Normal | Normal | Hypoxia is a late sign which may indicate imminent complete upper airway obstruction |

claims.claim: Stridor alone without change in behaviour or work of breathing may not require urgent intervention
claims.source_text: stridor alone, without change in behaviour, work of breathing, etc, may not require urgent intervention

claims.claim: The differential diagnosis includes retropharyngeal abscess, peritonsillar abscess or quinsy, bacterial tracheitis, epiglottitis, and airway burns or trauma
claims.source_text: Retropharyngeal abscess … Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) … Bacterial tracheitis … Epiglottitis … Airway burns or trauma

claims.claim: Croup is a clinical diagnosis and investigations such as respiratory swab or nasopharyngeal aspirate, X-rays and blood tests are not indicated in typical presentations, with appropriate investigations considered if there is concern for differential diagnoses
claims.source_text: Croup is a clinical diagnosis. Investigations such as respiratory swab or nasopharyngeal aspirate, X-rays and blood tests are **not** indicated in typical presentations. Consider appropriate investigations if there is concern for differential diagnoses as above

claims.claim: Clinicians should minimise distress to avoid worsening symptoms and minimise interventions including examination and investigation that are not going to impact acute management, keep the child with carers to reduce distress, and try to keep the environment quiet with moderate lighting
claims.source_text: **Minimise distress** to avoid worsening symptoms, minimise interventions including examination and investigation that are not going to impact acute management … Keep child with carers to reduce distress … Try to keep the environment quiet, moderate lighting

claims.claim: Children will adopt a position of comfort that minimises airway obstruction and this should not be changed
claims.source_text: Children will adopt a position of comfort that minimises airway obstruction, do not change this

claims.claim: Supplemental oxygen is not usually required, and if needed the child should be managed as severe upper airway obstruction or an alternative diagnosis such as anaphylaxis or asthma considered
claims.source_text: Supplemental oxygen is not usually required. If needed, manage as severe upper airway obstruction or consider alternative diagnosis eg anaphylaxis, asthma

claims.claim: Children with barking cough alone and no history of stridor do not require steroids
claims.source_text: Children with barking cough alone and no history of stridor do not require steroids

claims.claim: In mild croup oral steroids of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral or prednisolone 1 mg/kg oral should be considered if stridor is present or if there are risk factors such as young age and inability to access urgent review
claims.source_text: Consider oral steroids: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral or prednisolone 1 mg/kg oral if stridor present or if risk factors such as young age and inability to access urgent review

claims.claim: In moderate croup oral steroids of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral or prednisolone 1 mg/kg oral are given, with nebulised adrenaline considered if symptoms are persistent or worsening
claims.source_text: Oral steroids: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral or prednisolone 1 mg/kg oral … Consider nebulised adrenaline if persistent or worsening symptoms

claims.claim: In severe croup there should be senior clinician review with management in a high acuity treatment area, nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg to a maximum of 12 mg by oral, intramuscular or intravenous route
claims.source_text: Senior clinician review. Manage in high acuity treatment area … Nebulised adrenaline **and** … Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg) PO/IM/IV

claims.claim: In life-threatening croup the child should be moved to a resuscitation area with senior staff involved, given nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000, 100 per cent oxygen at 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask, and dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg to a maximum of 12 mg intramuscularly or intravenously
claims.source_text: Move to resuscitation area and involve senior staff … Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 … 100% oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask … Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg) IM/IV

claims.claim: Further doses of nebulised adrenaline can be given until a senior clinician is available to provide airway support
claims.source_text: Further doses of nebulised adrenaline can be given until senior clinician available to provide airway support

claims.claim: Children can be discharged home once stridor free at rest, and a period of observation of 3 hours is required after nebulised adrenaline to ensure no recurrence of symptoms
claims.source_text: Children can be discharged home once stridor free at rest … A period of observation of 3 hours is required after nebulised adrenaline to ensure no recurrence of symptoms

claims.claim: A longer period of observation than 3 hours should be considered for a child who presents overnight, has limited access to medical care, presents with stridor more than once during the same illness, or has risk factors for severe croup
claims.source_text: presents overnight … has limited access to medical care … presents with stridor more than once during the same illness … has risk factors for severe croup

claims.claim: Consultation with the local paediatric team should be considered where severe airway obstruction is present, the child has risk factors or there is any doubt about diagnosis, the child is less than 6 months of age, or there is no improvement with nebulised adrenaline
claims.source_text: Severe airway obstruction present … Child has risk factors or any doubt about diagnosis … Child less than 6 months of age … No improvement with nebulised adrenaline

claims.claim: Transfer should be considered where there is no improvement following nebulised adrenaline, the child requires repeated doses of nebulised adrenaline, or the child requires care above the level of comfort of the local hospital
claims.source_text: No improvement following nebulised adrenaline … Child requiring repeated doses of nebulised adrenaline … Child requiring care above the level of comfort of the local hospital

claims.claim: Discharge requires a minimum of 3 hours observation post nebulised adrenaline if this has been required, and parents should be advised to seek medical attention if there is recurrence of stridor at rest despite having received oral steroids
claims.source_text: Minimum of 3 hours observation post nebulised adrenaline (if this has been required) … Parents should be advised to seek medical attention if recurrence of stridor at rest despite having received oral steroids

claims.claim: Antibiotics have no role in uncomplicated croup as it has a viral aetiology
claims.source_text: Antibiotics have no role in uncomplicated croup as it has a viral aetiology

claims.claim: Anti-tussives such as codeine have no proven effect on the course or severity of croup and may cause respiratory depression and increase sedation
claims.source_text: Anti-tussives such as codeine have no proven effect on the course or severity of croup, and may cause respiratory depression and increase sedation

claims.claim: Cold air exposure below 10 degrees Celsius might reduce severity in moderate croup, humidified air has not been proven to change the severity of croup, and heliox has not been shown to be better than nebulised adrenaline in severe croup
claims.source_text: Cold air (below 10 degC) exposure might reduce severity in moderate croup … Humidified air has not been proven to change the severity of croup … Heliox has not been shown to be better than nebulised adrenaline in severe croup

claims.claim: The guideline was last updated September 2024 and is PIC endorsed
claims.source_text: Last updated September 2024 … PIC Endorsed

claims.claim: The guideline cites a Cochrane review of glucocorticoids for croup in children and a 2023 randomised controlled trial of outdoor cold air versus room temperature exposure for croup symptoms
claims.source_text: Aregbesola A, Tam CM, Kothari A, Le ML, Ragheb M, Klassen TP. Glucocorticoids for croup in children. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2023 … Siebert JN, Salomon C, Taddeo I, Gervaix A, Combescure C, Lacroix L. Outdoor Cold Air Versus Room Temperature Exposure for Croup Symptoms: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Pediatrics. 2023

claims.claim: The diagram states that in mild croup no steroids may be considered if there is barking cough alone, and that if there is a history of stridor or risk factors, dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral or prednisolone 1 mg/kg oral should be considered with a repeat dose the following evening
claims.source_text: Mild / Consider no steroids if barking cough alone / If history of stridor, or risk factors, consider: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral or Prednisolone 1 mg/kg oral, repeat dose following evening

claims.claim: The diagram states that in moderate croup dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral or prednisolone 1 mg/kg oral is given with a repeat dose the following evening
claims.source_text: Moderate / Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral or Prednisolone 1 mg/kg oral with a repeat dose the following evening

claims.claim: The diagram states that nebulised budesonide 2 mg should be considered if oral corticosteroids are not tolerated
claims.source_text: *Consider nebulised budesonide 2 mg if oral corticosteroids not tolerated

claims.claim: In the diagram a good response to moderate treatment leads to discharge home once stridor free at rest, and deterioration leads to the severe pathway
claims.source_text: Good response / Discharge home once stridor free at rest / Deterioration

claims.claim: The diagram states that severe croup is treated with nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of undiluted adrenaline 1:1000 and dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg to a maximum of 12 mg by intramuscular, intravenous or oral route
claims.source_text: Severe / Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of undiluted adrenaline 1:1000 and Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg) IM/IV/PO

claims.claim: In the diagram a good response to severe treatment means repeating the adrenaline dose if there is recurrence of severe respiratory distress, and considering discharge at 3 hours post adrenaline if stridor free at rest
claims.source_text: Good response / Repeat adrenaline dose if recurrence of severe respiratory distress / Consider discharge at 3 hours post adrenaline if stridor free at rest

claims.claim: In the diagram a minimal or poor response to severe treatment means repeating the dose of adrenaline, considering an alternative diagnosis, and escalation to senior staff or ICU
claims.source_text: Minimal or poor response / Repeat dose of adrenaline / Consider alternative diagnosis / Escalation to senior/ICU

claims.claim: The diagram states that life-threatening croup requires immediate senior involvement, ICU or anaesthetics, nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of undiluted adrenaline 1:1000, oxygen at 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask, and dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg to a maximum of 12 mg intramuscularly or intravenously
claims.source_text: Life-threatening / Immediate senior involvement/ICU/anaesthetics / Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of undiluted adrenaline 1:1000 / Oxygen 15 L/min via non rebreather mask / Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg) IM/IV
